AGRIevance

By: Anina Peens | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We go undercover to the Potchefstroom Agricultural college to investigate the run-down broken mess the country’s agricultural colleges have become.

Unique Selling Point:
Built to ensure food security, create employment and uplift communities, the country's state owned agricultural colleges, once the pride and joy of the sector, have dilapidated into a complete state of decay... and the students have to bear the brunt.

Summary:
Students at the Potchefstroom agricultural college were supposed to learn about dairy, but for the last three years, there was only one cow, and she has now died of mastitis. Most of the country’s eleven state owned agricultural colleges are in a dilapidated state of decay and students have to revert to strike action to receive lectures. This, while politically appointed lecturers are selling the livestock, they are supposed to use in training of young farmers.


Further information:
On their websites, they sell the ultimate farming dream, offering training in dairy farming, fruit farming, tree growing, agronomy, you name it, they offer it. But most importantly, the colleges offer practical placements and integrated learning programees; a drawing card for students. But once the students enroll and get to campus, reality has a different face. The college buildings are dilapidated, have no farming equipment, laboratories, hardly any lectures, no running water or clean and adequate sanitary facilities. The students have to arrange their own practical excursions and cover the cost. At most of the centers, there is no livestock left. The few animals used for practical training are thin, underfed and sick.
For years, there was only one dairy cow at the Potchefstroom campus, and she has now died of neglect and disease.
At the Potchefstroom, Taung and Tompi Seleka colleges, livestock is sold by the lecturers- especially chickens and eggs have regular buyers.
For students who want to specialize in sheep farming, there are no sheep on campus…they have all been stolen, sold or died of disease and hunger.
The colleges don’t arrange field trips and if there are any outings to farms, the students have to arrange it themselves and cover their own costs.
The colleges fall under the provincial management of each province, and is funded by the department of agriculture, land reform and rural development (DALRRD). Students say, due to political appointments, there is no real knowledge of agri training, and they are sitting in classes where they learn nothing. Classes are also cancelled without notice and schedules are changed at the leisure of the lecturers. At Taung and Potchefstroom, students are planning to embark on strike action to bring their grievances to national attention.

But that is not where it ends.
About 5000 students graduate every year from these colleges, mostly through self-study. Just over 1300 of them are then placed on farms by DALRRD. Each student receives a stipend of R7000.
The farmers hosting the students are paid large sums of money to train the students for a period of two years. But students say, the living and working conditions are dreadful, and graduates are treated as cheap laborers despite their tertiary qualifications. One student tells us how he was placed on a farm under the impression that he would learn about farming economics, equipment, science and labor practice but ended up planting spinach every day, for two years. Due to a lack of practical experience, he can only be hired as a farm worker and can never truly realize his dream to manage a farm or aspire to become a commercial farmer.
This is not only sad for youth like Mologadi who battles to fulfill her dream, but also ironic for a government that pays a lot of lip service to land reform, black economic empowerment and developing young black farmers. Some students say, while they are telling government that they are available and willing to grow in agriculture, ANC cadres get all the opportunities. The provincial structures take farms and give it to their friends and family while there is a pool of young dynamic black youth, desperately waiting for opportunities they won’t get if the state does not help. Many of the students won’t inherit farms from their families and government is their only hope to becoming commercial farmers. But government does not want the youth close because they are scared, they will be exposed, some students say; “they are scared we reveal the corruption and show how the steal the money allocated for our education and development”.
There are inspectors who are supposed to visit the schools and farms and report back to DALRRD about practical progress of the students, but these inspectors are apparently bribed by the landowners to write false reports.
The two-year placement period is used to drive up numbers for employment stats and in the end, the graduates fall into the unemployment pool, once their two-year practical have lapsed.

Together with a couple of students from other colleges, Mologadi established SAAGA, the South African agricultural graduates association in 2020, an NPO, representing agricultural students across the country who share similar grievances. SAAGA aims to connect with government as the voice of the black farming youth. But its president Malose Mokgoto who manages SAAGA from his home in Soweto says, government keeps shutting the door in his face. SAAGA, who has no membership fee or income, represents 15 thousand Agri students countrywide. They have written letters to the president, they have had meetings with the DALLRD, pleading with Minister Thoko Didiza and her delegates to include their voices in policy making, consider them when making decisions, assist them in saving the colleges, eradicate corruption in provincial Agri structures, appoint trained staff, sort out admin and help them to become farmers…all without any success.

List of colleges:

Functioning colleges:

- Elsensburg- Stellenbosch WC
- Cedara college of agriculture- Hilton KZN
- Bolland college – Caledon, Paarl, Stellenbosch, Strand, Worcester

Dysfunctional colleges:

- Potchefstroom College of Agriculture- Potchefstroom NW
- Glen college of agriculture- Bloemfontein
- Lowveld college of agriculture- Mbombela
- Madzivhandila college of agriculture – Tohoyandou, Venda
- Tompi Seleka college- Marblehall, Limpopo
- Weston agricultural college – Greytown, KZN
- Taung college of agri – Taung NW
- Fort Cox college of agriculture and forestry- King Williams Town, Eastern Cape

Student Grievances

- Lack of lectures/changed and canceled lectures
- Staff and lecturers order fodder/ equipment/ laptops and cellphones for students but they never receive it.
- No farming equipment for practicals
- No animals for practicals
- No study material
- Instead of arranging integrated learning programs, lecturers thumb suck marks
- Semesters shortened from six months to two months
- Enrolled for poultry course but the chickens are all sold by the staff
- Hostels are dilapidated, especially at Venda: no running water, one toilet to share between all students, old food
- No burseries
- No wifi
- Insufficient staff
- No sport facilities or events
- No online learning/registration or comms

Script:


AGRIEVANCE
NEW SCRIPT IN TWO PARTS

VO 
There are eleven specialist agricultural colleges in South Africa. Owned by the state, they were all built between 1905 and 1982. For longer than a century these schools that- specialize in practical hands-on learning- have produced many commercial farmers. 

SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE: AGRISA
“Your colleges are supposed to teach your students all the practicalities that they require…
MAC: TO BE A PLAASBOER 
To be a farmer, especially for a student that has not been exposed to agriculture. 

VO
Established in 1909, Potchefstroom college of agriculture is the second oldest of the eleven institutions, its students fondly nicknamed Pampoenboere. It was once world-renowned, synonymous with agricultural excellence. Sadly, for the more representative student body of today, and as is the case with most of the other 11 institutions, that picture has changed. 

UPSOUND 
SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE: AGRISA
“The majority of those colleges are dysfunctional”

VO
The department of agriculture land reform and rural development provides the bulk funding for all the colleges. So, as long as students enrol, funding keeps coming. On their websites, the colleges offer hands-on training to students but, once enrolled at some of these colleges, reality quickly sets in. 

USE DIFFERENT VISUALS HERE. USE ONLY THE AUDIO AND PLACE IT OVER THE DIRTY ANIMAL ENCLOSURES
UPSOUND
POTCH 0338 
SUBTITLE AND BLEEP
“We don’t learn about animal health. We basically just clean the s***”

VO 
These pictures of derelict buildings in the Potchefstroom campus shared on social media first attracted our attention. We set out to see things for ourselves. While undercover on campus, the student representative council or SRC shows us around. This cellphone footage  shows what seems to be considerable neglect.
VO 
Poor administration and campus neglect have been problems for years. AgriSA was part of a 2016 task team that worked on numerous problems experienced at most of the colleges. 
 
SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE: AGRISA
“…you got a student, worker, ratio problem. In some instances, there are more workers at those colleges than students. So, your funding is completely skewed, it lands up in the pockets of lectures and staff”

VO 
Malusi Makgatla holds a degree in agricultural science, but he’ s a novelist because his dreams of becoming a commercial farmer were dashed. He started a national student movement called SAAGA, an agricultural graduates association.

SUPER@ MALUSE MAKGATLA: PRESIDENT SAAGA
“There is not transparency and openness. There is a lot of corruption, they are not open to the school SRC’s”

VO 
Malose manages SAAGA from his home in Soweto without any financial support, trying to raise student grievances with the government. 

SUPER@ MALOSE MAKGATHLA: PRESIDENT: SAAGA
75 
“We hear grievances from graduates all around the country and we are trying to engage the department, but you know, out administration in the government is shallow, they don’t take us seriously. They think, they are arrogant. They are only care about themselves. 

VO 
Malose says the absence of transparency is an ongoing issue for the SRC’s from North West and Limpopo, but even worse is the lack of practical training, the very thing the colleges were built for. 

visual transition to Venda

VO 
Malose tells us, in deep rural Venda at the Madzivhandila college, students had to strike to get practical training. So we set off on the 5-hour journey to Thohoyandou. 

SUPER@ALERTHIA NKHUMELENI
BYTE IS SPLIT IN 2
“ I grew up in a family where they practice agriculture…

VO 
Second year student, Alerhtia Ngwakomonye, studies plant production. She comes from a family of farmers but wants to become a commercial farmer. 

SUPER@ALERTHIA NGWAKOMONYE: STUDENT
“I decided to come here to Madzivhandila agricultural college because I saw it on the internet, and I was like, ok let me go and then I arrived here and I was like, urhg, the things I see in the prospectus are different. We don’t have practicals”

VO 
Fourth-year student, Mulwli Phaswana, echoes this agrees. He owns a farm, but decided to enroll at the Madzivhandila college, to develop commercial farming skills. But, like Alerthia, he was gravely disappointed.
(PASUE)
The SRC gives us a tour of campus, starting at the boarding facilities

SUPER@ MULWELI PHASWANA: STUDENT
“This is our kitchen, where we get our meals. This is what AgriSETA is paying for. This is what DAFF is paying for. Whoever that is giving us bursaries paying for our meals, this is what they are paying for”

“You may find that the timetable for meals is offering you one boiled egg and four slices of dry bread”

“And this is the state of the kitchen. There is the timetable for what we eat. 
MAC: OH WITH COCKROACHES?!” (BREATH for several beats)
VO 
College staff scramble to clean the kitchen as we enter, but there’s clearly not enough time to cover things up. 

UPSOUND
“Here we have the meat, cooldrinks…what’s this? This is beetroot, I guess. 
MAC: AND ONE CHEESE FOR 160 STUDENTS.

VO 
Madzivhandila college receives just under 60 million Rand from the government every year and the sector’s training authority, AgriSETA, pays forty thousand Rand per student, per semester. Most students are bursary funded. If AgriSeta funds just 50 students twice a year, we estimate at least four million Rand should be available to cater for food, residences and maintenance.

SUPER@ MULWELI PHASWANA: STUDENT
“We striked for maintenance of this residence and they appoint service providers to come and do renovations. So, when they came to do the renovations, we thought that they are going to improvise this, fix it… you see, these toilets are old”

VO 
And as we’re filming, we’re once again stopped by security demanding we switch off our cameras, saying the SRC isn’t allowed to show us around.
We’re escorted to the office, where principle, Khathu Madau, refuses to come out and address us. meet us.

MAC: DO YOU WANT US TO COME WITH THE SRC?
ANINA: WE COME WITH OUR CAMERA
SECURITY: NO, YOU DON’T NEED THE CAMERA INSIDE.
ANINA: WE COME WITH OUR CAMERA 
SECURITY: NO YOU DON’T NEED THE CAMERA ASSEBLIEF
PART OF SEABI IS OUT AND MERGED. PLEASE REPLACE ENTIRE PARAGRAPH 

VO 
COMING UP AFTER THE break: SECURITY GUARDS BLOCK OUR cameras AS students REVEAL more on THE DIRE STATE OF AGRICULTURAL TRAINING THAT your taxes are supposed to pay for.

END OF PART 1 

PART 2

VISUAL RECAP OF PART 1: 
Eleven state-owned agricultural colleges, funded by our tax Rands, are meant to provide practical training for a new generation of farmers in a nation desperate for land reform. 
But, is the government taking young people in agriculture seriously? 


VISUAL SEGUE BACK TO VENDA: 
Madzivhandila college in Tohoyhandou, Venda, was once a jewel in the fertile Levhubu river valley famous for a variety of tropical fruits. It could be a doorway to commercial farming for students from impoverished rural villages. 

LINK
Thohoyandou is a treasure trove of agricultural opportunity, you can literally grow anything here, from tropical fruit and vegetables to livestock and you can create job opportunities. But the biggest challenge is the training of commercial farmers.

VO 
The Madzivhadila college was established in 1982,– Today, it still receives millions of Rands from the government to train young farmers…But students say they learn nothing. 

UPSOUND
SUBTITLE
MAC: So when you are supposed to do practical, what do the lecturers say?
PRINCE: Practicals You are talking about practicals?
STUDENT: WE JUST GOOGLE. 
MAC: OH YOUTUBE VIDEOS?

VO 
A revealing campus tour, led by fourth year student, Mulweli Pashwana, and the SRC is cut short as college management demands that we switch off our cameras. 

UPSOUND: REPEAT OF UPSOUND AT END OF PART 1: NO CAMERAS ASSEBLIEF 

VO 
College PRINCIPAL Khathu Madau doesn't want to talk to us outside and insists we get permission to film from the provincial spokesperson of the department of agriculture nearly three hours away in Polokwane. The spokesperson will give permission only if the principle clears it. We wait for them, waiting for each other.
(PAUSE)
Outside, the students grow agitated and when security tries to block our cameras once more, they march into the boardroom.

UPSOUND 
“No I am sorry, I invited these people in.
PRINCIPLE: NO, NOT WITH THE CAMERA BUT WITH YOURSELF. WE MEET WITH THEM BUT NOT WITH THE MEDIA 
“I am subscribed to the college…”
“You keep this college declining and it is our future…principle please plead with us… we are your students”

MAC EXTENDED, PRINCIPLE MOVED DOWN
Mac: principal, do you know the issues that these students are raising? all of these things? 
LET US HEAR THE GRIEVANCES OF THE CHILDREN OF THE STUDENTS AND SEE WHAT IS HAPPENING… 
PRINCIPLE: I DON’T HAVE PROBLEM IF YOU CANT WAIT 
Mac: So you know what is the beautiful thing about the youth? like the youth of 1976, they don’t have time to wait. 
MAC: we don’t have time to wait for bureaucracy and communications and emails. these are their futures all of these children, it is their future that people are messing around with. they sit with their suits in Polokwane making decisions writing emails. 
Principle: I don’t have problem if you can’t wait 
Mac: Let us hear the grievances of the children of the students and see what is happening. 
MULWELI: Mac, the very same people you are waiting for are the people who are corrupt….

VO 
Principal Mudau refuses to hear the students out. With security still trying to block our cameras, the students lead us further into the campus.

UPSOUND
MAC: THE STRUGGLE CONTINUES

VO 
They show us their books. Those studying animal health and production say they’ve never set foot inside in the college’s laboratories. 

UPSOUND
MAC: YOU CAN CLEARLY SEE THAT THIS HAS NEVER BEEN USED. NOBODY HAS EVER BEEN IN THIS LAB. THERE IS STILL DUST. LOOK AT THIS. 

MULWELI: Have you ever been in here? you are doing animal nutrition? You did basic animal and plant sciences?
STUDENT: Yes. 
PRINCE: you have to know the inside of a chicken and what is going on inside a chicken but you have never came to make operations and see?
STUDENT: It is the first time

UPSOUND ALERTHIA
SUBTITLE
We are doing soil classification. I have to know about the soil, the PH. The colour, I don’t know anything. 

VO 
Students who study crop production tell us they have only ever planted spinach and maize - which the college staff then grab

MAC: SO, THEY ARE EVEN RUNNING THEIR OWN LITTLE INTERNAL BUSINESSES 

UPSOUND: MULWELI
“As students, we go there and we work hard. After that, they will go there and they will harvest our vegetables and sell amongst themselves… you know, they are eating lunch”

VO 
In 2016, a task team sent by the department of agriculture land reform and rural development looked into the state of the colleges. Agriculture federation, AGRISA, was part of that team which found- even then- that students weren’t getting sufficient practical training. Questions were raised about the appointment of lecturers. 

SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE: CEO: AGRISA
“…there is a big question mark about the quality of the qualifications of many of the lecturers whether they do have the necessary qualifications in agriculture to transfer knowledge to those students” 

VO 
While at the college, we don’t see a single lecturer on campus. The matron, who’s supposed to look after the students in residence, is nowhere to be found. But how is practical training even possible when the college doesn’t have enough farm animals?

BREATHER

VO
These chicken pens WERE erected on a college sports field. There hasn't been one chicken on campus in two years. Students say they get practical marks for cleaning the pens.

Things are no better at the milk production plant

UPSOUND

MAC: For 160 students that are learning about cows, they’ve got only one cow.

Mulweli
“How much money are they claiming on that invoice to buy feeds for this one cattle. Does the department recognize that it is only one cattle here?

VO 
The Limpopo department of agriculture, land reform and rural development answered our questions on behalf of the college principal… “practical training” they say,  is done outside the college on small stock farms. 

VO 
So, what about the facilities and infrastructure funded by taxpayers? funded?

UPSOUND MULWELI
44
Mac this was constructed three or four years ago. And the people who were given the tenders were paid off. Meaning that the job is well done. We came here to conduct the processing practical, but no machine is working here. 
MAC: THIS IS ALL NEW MACHINERY
“Ja they are rusting”
45
MAC: YOU KNOW IT WOULD BE ONE THING IF YOU WENT TO A COLLEGE AND THERE WAS NOTHING. YOU HAVE GOT THE FACILITIES. THESE ARE WORLD CLASS I HAVE SEEN IT ON COMMERCIAL FARMS, BUT YOU GUYS HAVE NEVER EVER USED IT?  THIS IS A TRAVESTY, I MEAN IT IS UNBELIEVABLE THAT GOVERNMENT IS ALLOWING FOR THIS TO HAPPEN

VO
The collapse of these colleges has far-reaching CONSEQUENCEs. Once the students graduate, the government funds them for further internships on commercial farms.  

SUPER@ MALOSE MAKGATLA
“They don’t even have practical, conducive, thick knowledge, they fail to perform outside, there. Then the farmers treat them like general laborers and that is a problem, they are professionals”. 

VO 
For students graduating from colleges such as Madzivandila, it will be challenging carving out a career in the commercial farming sector. 

SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE
“They take note of your cv and where you were trained and if the industry has any suspicion that the quality of training at a particular college, then that CV is discarded” 

VO 
Ten million hectares of farmland is under the custodianship of the state. Students say, this land should be made available to agri graduates. 

UPSOUND MULWELI: 
66
Politicians, they keep on talking, but they need everything for their interest. When they get the land back, they will forget to do the production. They will never think of an African kid who need an employment from the land. They are collapsing it”

END

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We go undercover to the Potchefstroom Agricultural college to investigate the run-down broken mess the country’s agricultural colleges have become.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Built to ensure food security, create employment and uplift communities, the country's state owned agricultural colleges, once the pride and joy of the sector, have dilapidated into a complete state of decay... and the students have to bear the brunt.
metadata.Summary: Students at the Potchefstroom agricultural college were supposed to learn about dairy, but for the last three years, there was only one cow, and she has now died of mastitis. Most of the country’s eleven state owned agricultural colleges are in a dilapidated state of decay and students have to revert to strike action to receive lectures. This, while politically appointed lecturers are selling the livestock, they are supposed to use in training of young farmers.
metadata.Further information: On their websites, they sell the ultimate farming dream, offering training in dairy farming, fruit farming, tree growing, agronomy, you name it, they offer it. But most importantly, the colleges offer practical placements and integrated learning programees; a drawing card for students. But once the students enroll and get to campus, reality has a different face. The college buildings are dilapidated, have no farming equipment, laboratories, hardly any lectures, no running water or clean and adequate sanitary facilities. The students have to arrange their own practical excursions and cover the cost. At most of the centers, there is no livestock left. The few animals used for practical training are thin, underfed and sick. For years, there was only one dairy cow at the Potchefstroom campus, and she has now died of neglect and disease. At the Potchefstroom, Taung and Tompi Seleka colleges, livestock is sold by the lecturers- especially chickens and eggs have regular buyers. For students who want to specialize in sheep farming, there are no sheep on campus…they have all been stolen, sold or died of disease and hunger. The colleges don’t arrange field trips and if there are any outings to farms, the students have to arrange it themselves and cover their own costs. The colleges fall under the provincial management of each province, and is funded by the department of agriculture, land reform and rural development (DALRRD). Students say, due to political appointments, there is no real knowledge of agri training, and they are sitting in classes where they learn nothing. Classes are also cancelled without notice and schedules are changed at the leisure of the lecturers. At Taung and Potchefstroom, students are planning to embark on strike action to bring their grievances to national attention. But that is not where it ends. About 5000 students graduate every year from these colleges, mostly through self-study. Just over 1300 of them are then placed on farms by DALRRD. Each student receives a stipend of R7000. The farmers hosting the students are paid large sums of money to train the students for a period of two years. But students say, the living and working conditions are dreadful, and graduates are treated as cheap laborers despite their tertiary qualifications. One student tells us how he was placed on a farm under the impression that he would learn about farming economics, equipment, science and labor practice but ended up planting spinach every day, for two years. Due to a lack of practical experience, he can only be hired as a farm worker and can never truly realize his dream to manage a farm or aspire to become a commercial farmer. This is not only sad for youth like Mologadi who battles to fulfill her dream, but also ironic for a government that pays a lot of lip service to land reform, black economic empowerment and developing young black farmers. Some students say, while they are telling government that they are available and willing to grow in agriculture, ANC cadres get all the opportunities. The provincial structures take farms and give it to their friends and family while there is a pool of young dynamic black youth, desperately waiting for opportunities they won’t get if the state does not help. Many of the students won’t inherit farms from their families and government is their only hope to becoming commercial farmers. But government does not want the youth close because they are scared, they will be exposed, some students say; “they are scared we reveal the corruption and show how the steal the money allocated for our education and development”. There are inspectors who are supposed to visit the schools and farms and report back to DALRRD about practical progress of the students, but these inspectors are apparently bribed by the landowners to write false reports. The two-year placement period is used to drive up numbers for employment stats and in the end, the graduates fall into the unemployment pool, once their two-year practical have lapsed. Together with a couple of students from other colleges, Mologadi established SAAGA, the South African agricultural graduates association in 2020, an NPO, representing agricultural students across the country who share similar grievances. SAAGA aims to connect with government as the voice of the black farming youth. But its president Malose Mokgoto who manages SAAGA from his home in Soweto says, government keeps shutting the door in his face. SAAGA, who has no membership fee or income, represents 15 thousand Agri students countrywide. They have written letters to the president, they have had meetings with the DALLRD, pleading with Minister Thoko Didiza and her delegates to include their voices in policy making, consider them when making decisions, assist them in saving the colleges, eradicate corruption in provincial Agri structures, appoint trained staff, sort out admin and help them to become farmers…all without any success.
